The comparison that localises the defect is the model's output against the exact content sent in the request: agreement isolates it upstream in the tool's dependency, and disagreement would have isolated it in the model. That requires logging the content at the boundary rather than the call's name and status, which is the instrumentation gap that makes most origin questions unanswerable in practice. Second, detection. A silent truncation carries no error and no marker, so nothing in the protocol distinguishes it from a complete short record — and a summariser over an incomplete record produces a confident, wrong answer that the pipeline records as a success. So the harness has to establish completeness: check the returned length or item count against what the upstream reports, page the remainder, and surface an explicit incomplete-source signal to the model. The parallel with retrieval is exact — a wrapper that returns an empty result on timeout teaches the model that nothing exists, and a wrapper that returns a truncated bundle teaches it that the record ends there.

whyWrong.C: It asks the model to compensate for content it cannot know is missing. Nothing in the bundle signals incompleteness, so an instruction to watch for truncation cannot fire, and prompt changes cannot recover text that was never sent.
whyWrong.D: It claims the fault cannot be localised from the evidence in hand, when the comparison settles it directly. Agreement between the summary and the exact content sent is sufficient isolation; waiting for a multi-model experiment only delays a fix that is already locatable.

questions.mindset: A silent truncation is worse than an error: log content at the boundary to isolate it, then make the harness prove completeness so absence is never indistinguishable from a short record.

questions.scenario: Harrowgate Health's routing suite reports 96% pass. A developer inspects it and finds the grader asserts that the response is valid JSON — which the code path guarantees — and that no case exercises a referral the policy table does not cover.
questions.stem: What is wrong with the suite, and what is the correct repair?

options.text: The suite is measuring a property the system cannot fail, which is the worst kind of green: it consumes the run, blocks nothing, and would survive a change that broke every routing decision. The repair is to start from the property that matters — the routing decision is correct for this referral type under the current policy table — and express it as an assertion on the decision, not on the envelope. That means cases spanning the policy table's boundaries, and cases where the policy genuinely does not cover the referral, where the correct behaviour is a stated inability to route rather than a confident guess. Grading follows from the property: an exact-match assertion against a ground-truth decision where you have one, and support checks for the uncovered cases.
The suite is adequate because JSON validity is the contract the tool advertises. Consumers depend on the shape, so the shape is what should be guaranteed and tested.
The suite needs more cases rather than different assertions. Ninety-six per cent on a small set is an acceptable figure, and adding volume will tighten the estimate.
The uncovered-referral cases should be excluded, since behaviour outside the policy table is unspecified and testing it produces failures that no implementation can satisfy.

questions.explanation: The problem is not coverage volume, it is that the assertion targets a property the implementation guarantees for free. A JSON-validity check will pass on every run regardless of whether the routing decision was right, so the suite is expensive and inert — and the specific danger is that its green is indistinguishable from the green of a correct suite in every dashboard. The repair starts by naming the property that actually matters: for each referral, is the routing decision correct for that referral type under the current policy table. Then the assertions follow from that property rather than from the envelope. An exact-match check against a ground-truth decision is available wherever you have one, which is a deterministic grader and the strongest kind. And the uncovered cases are not unspecified — they are the ones where the correct behaviour is to say the referral is not covered, and asserting that is what prevents the system from confidently routing a case the policy does not address. That is the same design point as making absence representable in a schema: if 'not covered' is not an expected answer, the system cannot give it correctly.

whyWrong.B: It elevates the envelope to the contract and mistakes the cause. The shape being guaranteed is a consequence of how the response is produced; the routing decision is the thing consumers and members depend on, and it is unmeasured here.
whyWrong.C: It proposes more of the same measurement. Adding cases to an assertion that cannot fail produces a tighter estimate of a quantity nobody cares about.
whyWrong.D: It removes precisely the cases that catch the dangerous behaviour. Confidently routing a referral no policy covers is a high-severity error, and it is only detectable if the suite expects the inability to route.

questions.mindset: An assertion on a property the system cannot fail is inert green — assert the decision, include the cases the policy does not cover, and grade deterministically.

questions.scenario: Harrowgate Health runs a four-agent support system: a coordinator, a policy researcher, a benefits calculator and a writer. After an incident the team finds the trace contains four `request_id` values and no way to tell which agent or which tool call each belongs to.
questions.stem: What does a multi-agent run need in its trace, and what does the API give you to build it?

options.text: Each API call has its own `request_id` — in the `request-id` header and the `request_id` field of error bodies — so a four-agent run necessarily has four, and attribution has to be reconstructed by the harness rather than read off the API. That means recording, per call, the agent identity and the enclosing tool call id, alongside the `request_id`, and keeping the parent-child relationship as the calls nest. In the Agent SDK the natural join key is the tool-use id of the Agent or Skill call that started each subagent, and with forwarded subagent text in the output stream each subagent's messages carry a `parent_tool_use_id`, which makes the tree reconstructable. The run-level signal is separate and also needed: an exhausted `max_turns` or budget arrives as a distinct `ResultMessage` subtype such as `error_max_turns`, which is what tells you the run ended on a budget rather than on a decision.
A single run shares one `request_id` across all its calls, so the trace needs only that value plus the model. The four values the team found are the four agents' own identifiers.
The API returns a parent-child structure with agent names, so the correct fix is to log the response body as returned and parse it. No harness-side bookkeeping is required.
Agent identity should come from the `system` prompt, since each subagent runs its own system prompt from its definition file. Logging the first line of it identifies the agent.

questions.explanation: The API's unit is the call, not the run, so attribution is a harness responsibility and has to be designed. Every response carries its own unique `request-id` header and the same value as `request_id` in error bodies, which means a four-agent run has four identifiers and nothing in the response itself says which agent issued which. So the trace needs per-call agent identity and the enclosing tool-use id recorded next to the `request_id`, with the parent-child relationship preserved as calls nest — and there is a natural join key available, since a subagent is started by an Agent or Skill tool call whose id identifies it. In the Agent SDK, forwarding subagent text in the output stream makes each subagent's messages carry a `parent_tool_use_id`, which is what allows a nested delegation tree to be reconstructed from the stream rather than guessed at. Two supporting signals belong in the same trace: a subagent's context does not inherit the parent's conversation, so the delegation prompt is the only record of what it was told, and an exhausted turn or budget budget arrives as a distinct `ResultMessage` subtype — `error_max_turns` and the budget equivalent — which is what distinguishes a budget stop from a completed task.

whyWrong.B: It assumes request identity is per run. It is per response, so a multi-agent run necessarily produces several, and misreading them as agent identifiers inverts the relationship entirely.
whyWrong.C: It expects the response body to carry structure it does not contain. Nothing in a message identifies the issuing agent; the association exists only in the harness that issued the call.
whyWrong.D: It proposes deriving identity from prompt text. Subagents do run their own system prompts, but that is an implementation detail of how they are defined and is not a stable join key for attribution — and it breaks the moment two agents share a definition.

questions.mindset: One `request_id` per call, so attribute in the harness: log agent identity and the enclosing tool-use id, and use `parent_tool_use_id` to rebuild the tree.

questions.scenario: Harrowgate Health has fixed the routing defect and the failing referral now routes correctly when replayed. The team wants to declare the incident closed and asks what else is required before closing.
questions.stem: Which set of steps is required before this incident can be closed?

options.text: The replay is necessary and not sufficient. It establishes that the specific failure is fixed, on one input, in one environment. Before closing, the captured failing input becomes a permanent eval case with its expected behaviour so the class cannot return silently, the full suite is re-run — and again after any later prompt, code or model change, since those are the three things that can reintroduce it — and the eval's own noise floor is known well enough that the run's movement is interpretable. Then the operational pair: a runbook entry with detection, classification, response and verification, so the next occurrence is diagnosable rather than novel, and a bounded production check so the fix is confirmed under real traffic rather than only in replay. Only a bounded check, not an open-ended observation period, because an unquantified 'watch it for a week' is not a verification criterion.
The replay plus the full suite re-run is sufficient. Both the specific failure and the aggregate behaviour are now confirmed, so further verification adds latency to the close.
Close it now and open a follow-up ticket for the eval case. The defect is fixed and the eval work is not blocking, so splitting the work keeps the incident moving.
Close it only after an LLM judge confirms the routing is correct on the replayed input, since the deterministic replay cannot judge quality.

questions.explanation: The replay proves one thing: this input, in this environment, now routes correctly. Every other question about whether the fix holds is still open, and the plan's structure needs to close them in order. The first is regression coverage — turn the captured failing input and its expected behaviour into a permanent eval case, because that is what stops the same defect returning silently, and note that the suite must be re-run again after any later prompt, code or model change, since those are precisely the three things that can reintroduce a routing defect. The second is interpretability: you need to know the eval's noise floor well enough for the run's movement to mean something, or the confirmation is unfalsifiable. The third is operability — a runbook entry carrying detection, classification, response and verification, so the next occurrence is diagnosable rather than novel — and the fourth is confirmation under real traffic via a bounded check. Bounded is the operative word: an unquantified 'watch it for a while' is not a verification criterion, because there is no threshold at which you would conclude something went wrong.

whyWrong.B: It stops at the aggregate before the individual. A suite pass says nothing about whether the specific defect class is covered, so the one thing most likely to recur is the one thing left unguarded.
whyWrong.C: It defers the guard. An eval case written as a follow-up is an eval case that does not exist while the next change ships, which is the window in which a regression would land.
whyWrong.D: It adds a grader where a ground truth exists. Whether a referral routes to the right department is exactly checkable by assertion, so routing it through a model judge adds variance to a deterministic answer.

questions.mindset: A passing replay proves one input in one environment — close only after the eval case exists, the suite is re-run, the noise floor is known, and a bounded check confirms it.

questions.scenario: Harrowgate Health's agent reads a member's eligibility record with `check_eligibility`, reasons for about forty seconds, and then calls `disburse` using what it read. In that window an administrator suspends the member. The agent disburses against stale data and the pipeline records a success.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about this class of defect are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: The defect is a time-of-check to time-of-use problem, and retries do not address it. Neither the tool result nor the model is wrong about what it was told; what changed is the world between the read and the write. So the enforcement point has to be at the write: `disburse` re-checks the precondition it depends on and refuses if it no longer holds, returning a typed outcome that names the condition that changed rather than a generic conflict. This is the same reason a side-effecting write needs an idempotency key — both are about making the write safe against a world that moved, rather than about making the read more careful.

The fix is to shorten the reasoning window by capping the agent's turn count, so the elapsed time between read and write falls below the window in which the state can change. A tighter bound reduces the probability and is the cheapest available mitigation.

The fix is to make `check_eligibility` return a short-lived authorisation token rather than a boolean, and have `disburse` present it. The write is then bound to the state that was read, which removes the window entirely.

The pipeline should re-verify every disbursement asynchronously after the fact and reverse any that were against stale state. Post-hoc reconciliation is sufficient because the financial exposure per event is bounded.

questions.explanation: This is a distinct failure class from anything a retry policy addresses, and recognising it is the whole difficulty. The tool result was accurate when produced, the model reasoned correctly from it, and the pipeline recorded what actually happened — the defect is that the world changed inside the window between read and write. No amount of retry logic, turn limiting or better prompting closes a gap whose cause is external state mutation; the only effective move is to enforce the precondition at the point of the side effect. So `disburse` should re-check the condition it depends on and refuse if it no longer holds, returning a typed outcome naming the changed condition — which is the same reasoning that makes a side-effecting write need an idempotency key, since both are about making the write safe against a moving world. Token-based authorisation is the stronger version of that fix, because it binds the write to the specific state that was read rather than re-reading and hoping nothing changed again in the second window. Post-hoc reversal is the weakest, and its cost is borne by the member.

whyWrong.C: It proposes a tightening rather than an enforcement. A cap on turns shrinks the exposure window and still disburses against a state that was superseded — the failure becomes rarer, not impossible, and the remaining cases are silent.
whyWrong.D: It accepts a financial ceiling as a substitute for correctness. Asynchronous reversal means the member is paid and then clawed back, which is a different and worse outcome than not paying, and it does not stop the stale write.

questions.mindset: Time-of-check to time-of-use: enforce the precondition at the write — re-check it or bind it to the state that was read, because nothing upstream can close that window.

questions.scenario: Harrowgate Health's referral defect occurs in about 0.5% of referrals. The eval set has 400 cases and the current suite reports a single aggregate accuracy figure. The team wants to ship a prompt change that they believe fixes the defect and asks whether the suite will show it.
questions.stem: Which assessment of the suite's suitability is correct?

options.text: An aggregate over 400 cases is the wrong instrument for a 0.5% defect, in two distinct ways. It is underpowered: a change that fixes every instance of a rare defect moves the aggregate by a fraction of a point, which is indistinguishable from the run-to-run noise the team has already measured. And it is unattributable: even if the number moved, an average cannot tell you whether the movement came from the defect you targeted or from something unrelated. The right design is per-case paired comparison — run both configurations on the same cases and examine which cases flipped, with the target defect's cases called out specifically — plus a case set containing enough instances of the defect class to be meaningful, since two or three cases cannot support a claim about a 0.5% failure. Grading stays deterministic where a ground-truth decision exists.

The suite is suitable. A half per cent of four hundred cases is two cases, and an aggregate accuracy figure over the whole set is the standard way to evaluate a change, so the team should ship if the number does not fall.
The suite is suitable provided the threshold is loosened to accommodate the noise. A one-point band around the current figure would let a real improvement register without blocking unrelated changes.

The suite is unsuitable only because it lacks variety. Expanding to two thousand cases would give the resolution needed to detect a half-per-cent change, after which the existing aggregate figure becomes meaningful.

questions.explanation: Two properties fail independently, and fixing only one still leaves you unable to conclude anything. Power first: a defect at 0.5% means a perfect fix moves the aggregate by well under a point on a 400-case set, which sits inside the run-to-run variance the team has already measured — so a null result is uninformative rather than negative, and a positive result would be luck. Attribution second: even a movement you could detect in an average would not tell you whether it came from the cases you were targeting or from incidental variation elsewhere, because an aggregate is not decomposable. The design that answers the question is a paired comparison — both configurations on the same cases — with attention to which specific cases flipped and the target defect's cases identified explicitly, and with enough instances of the defect class in the set that a claim about it means something; two cases cannot support a statement about a half-per-cent failure. Grading stays deterministic where a ground-truth routing decision exists, since that is where the strongest signal is available.

whyWrong.B: It accepts the aggregate as informative while noting it contains two relevant cases. A figure that rests on two observations cannot support a decision about the change, and 'does not fall' is not a threshold.
whyWrong.C: It responds to underpowering by widening the acceptance band, which is the wrong direction. Loosening the band means the suite can no longer detect the regressions it exists to catch, so it trades the ability to see good changes for the ability to see bad ones.
whyWrong.D: It assumes the only deficiency is sample size. Even a large set leaves the aggregate unattributable — a real movement would still not be decomposable into the cases you targeted, so paired per-case comparison is required regardless of scale.

questions.mindset: A rare defect needs paired per-case comparison and enough instances of its class — an aggregate is both underpowered and unattributable, however large the set.

questions.scenario: Harrowgate Health is writing the escalation section of its runbook. The pipeline can queue, dead-letter or fail fast for every failure class. Leadership asks when a human should be paged rather than the pipeline handling it unattended.
questions.stem: Which escalation criterion is correct?

options.text: Page on the conditions where automated recovery cannot make progress and a human decision is genuinely required, and queue everything else. Concretely: a persistent 500 `api_error`, because the documented response is to contact support with the request ID and persistence is the signal; an authentication or billing failure, because only fixing the credential or the payment details clears it and no amount of retrying will; a spend-cap 429 with no `retry-after`, because it keeps failing until access resumes and someone must decide whether to raise the limit or stop usage. Everything else queues: transient 529s wait out their backoff, 413s are a scheduled payload fix with a known owner, and truncated responses are resent. Two design rules keep this honest — the queued work must be per-record and idempotent so nothing is lost or duplicated while it waits, and each queued entry has to carry its failure class so a class that never drains is visible as a class rather than as permanent backlog.
Page whenever any request fails. A human who sees every failure can prioritise better than the pipeline can.
Never page. Every documented failure class has a documented automated response, so paging a human only adds latency and trains the rota to ignore alerts.
Page based on volume thresholds alone, since volume is the only signal that is unambiguous. Classify errors as you queue them and let a human decide from the counts.

questions.explanation: The criterion is whether automated recovery can make progress, and it divides the documented classes cleanly. Persistent 500 `api_error` pages, because the documented response after backoff is to contact support with the request ID — persistence is the escalation signal and the request ID is what makes the escalation actionable. Authentication and billing failures page for the same structural reason: only fixing the credential or the payment details clears them, so retrying cannot help and the pipeline's only honest options are queue or fail. A spend-cap 429 without `retry-after` pages too, because it keeps failing until access resumes and someone must decide whether to raise the limit or reduce usage. The rest queues rather than pages, because time and code changes resolve them: 529 is temporary capacity pressure, 413 is a hard payload ceiling with a known owner and a known fix, and truncated responses are resent with a higher `max_tokens`. Volume-only paging fails because it cannot distinguish a spend cap from a brief 529 burst, and never paging fails because it discards the classes where a human decision is the only possible progress.

whyWrong.B: It pages on everything, which produces alert fatigue and destroys the signal. Most failures are transient and resolve themselves, so a page per failure trains the rota to ignore the pages that matter.
whyWrong.C: It claims every class has an automated response, which is false for the classes that require a human decision. A revoked key, a failed payment and a spend cap are not resolved by any retry, and a system that cannot express 'a human must decide' will either retry forever or drop work silently.
whyWrong.D: It reduces escalation to volume, which cannot separate the classes. A brief 529 burst can outnumber a spend cap by orders of magnitude while being the one that requires no human at all.

questions.mindset: Page only where no automated response can make progress; queue everything else per-record and idempotently, carrying the failure class so a stuck class is visible.
